rationale: THE UNIT. Every other number here is a multiple of one click. These are RELATIVE units, not seconds or milliseconds - never report a total as a time estimate. A score is only meaningful next to another score of the same flow.

Two presses but one aim: the second acquisition has distance ~0, so it costs well under two clicks. If you cannot tell from the recording whether a double-click was intended, count two clicks and say so in the ledger.

Press, track the target under continuous visual correction, release. Aiming is paid twice and a slip loses the whole gesture. If the drag has a click-based alternative in the same view, count the cheaper path - the human will find it.

One viewport height of deliberate scrolling. Motorically cheap, but it pushes content out of view and anything still needed from above becomes a memory item. Count that separately; do not fold it in here.
Per character actually typed. Ten characters cost one click. Do not count characters the system filled in - a pre-filled field the user accepts unchanged costs field-entry only.

Focus a field, confirm the value is right, commit. Use for pickers, checkboxes, toggles and pre-filled fields where nothing is typed. If the user retypes a pre-filled value, it is field-entry-typed instead.

Overhead of a field the user must produce a value for: recall it, format it, survive validation. Count keystroke-char ON TOP for the characters. Never charge both field-entry and field-entry-typed for one field.

Open, scan, pick from <=7 visible options. This is the motor and scanning cost only. The classification cost is a decision-* row and is counted as well - they measure different things and charging both is correct, not double-counting.

Same act over a list that does not fit the viewport: scanning becomes searching. If the control has type-ahead AND the user used it, charge select-from-short-list plus the keystrokes - filtering is what makes a 200-item list survivable.

Anchor jump, in-page tab, accordion, expand. Content changes but the shell and the user's sense of place survive. If the URL changes and the header reloads, it is navigation-new-page regardless of what the router calls it.
Full context replacement: the user re-orients, re-scans, and loses their place in the old screen. Wait time is a separate wait-* row - a fast navigation is still a navigation.

A modal interrupts at whatever moment it fires and blocks the surface behind it. If it opened without the user asking (a promo, a nag, an unrequested tour), charge it AND flag the finding - an uninvited interrupt can flush what the user was holding.

Finding the exit costs more than pressing it, and users hesitate when it is unclear whether dismissing discards their work. If the dismiss control is ambiguous, charge a read-instruction on top and record why.

An in-app tab hides its sibling. Anything the user needed from the tab they left is now a memory-item-carried - count it. If the two tabs are never needed together, this is cheap and the finding is elsewhere.

Leaving the product entirely - email client, authenticator, spreadsheet, PDF - and coming back. The task context decays while the user is away and must be rebuilt on return. This is the most expensive routine act in most real flows.

Free by definition. Inside the Doherty band the user never leaves the loop, so the model must score it as zero - otherwise shaving 300ms off a 200ms response reads as a win it is not. Optimise the waits that are actually costing something.

Noticed, but thought flow survives (Miller's second threshold). Needs an indeterminate indicator by ~400ms. If nothing acknowledges the click at all, charge wait-2s-10s instead - unacknowledged waiting feels far longer than it is.
The user knows they are waiting and is watching a spinner. Costs four clicks because attention is held hostage and nothing is being accomplished. Needs determinate progress with a label by ~2s.

Attention departs and the task state has to be rebuilt on return - the cost is re-acquisition, not the clock. Deliberately far above its share of wall time. A wait this long needs a backgrounded, resumable, notify-me model, not a bigger spinner.

One fact the user must hold across a screen boundary because the system would not hold it: an order number, a code, a value being compared. Five clicks each, so a fourth item costs 20 - which is the point. Past four the flow is over budget, not merely heavy.

Going back a step the user did not intend to revisit - browser back, wizard previous, reopening a completed section. Includes re-orientation. Charge the forward steps again as they are repeated; backtrack is only the reversal itself.

A rejection arriving at the moment of highest commitment. Expensive because of what it does to confidence, not because of the pixels. Charge it once per rejection, even when several fields fail at once - one submit, one hit.

Fixed overhead of reading the message, working out what it actually wants, and re-committing. The literal re-typing and re-clicking are counted normally on top. If the user could not recover and abandoned, do not charge this - report the abandonment.

One visible undo that fully reverses the act. Cheap on purpose: a flow with real undo is a cheaper flow, and the model should reward shipping it. Requires the undo to be discoverable at the moment of the mistake, not buried in a menu.

No single undo exists, so the user reverses by hand across several screens and can never be sure they got it all. That residual uncertainty is most of the cost. If reversal is not possible at all, it is irreversible-action instead.

Deliberately far larger than the click that performs it. Fear is not local: once a user knows this screen can destroy something, they slow down, re-read, and second-guess everywhere on it. Charge it wherever the user cannot tell that an act is safe, not only where it truly is not.

A modal plus a decision, and the weaker mitigation - it lowers the slip rate but not the fear, so it does NOT discount irreversible-action. Charge both. Undo is the cheaper fix and usually the right proposal.

Scrolling while visually hunting for something not currently on screen. Distinct from scroll-screen, which is just travel. Finding a control routinely costs more than moving to it, and no motor law covers that half - this row is where it lands.

Formulating a query is recall, and recall is the expensive mode. Covers composing and committing the search; count keystroke-char for the query text and a select-* row for picking from the results. If the user searched because navigation failed them, that is the finding.

Per block of helper text, tooltip, or inline explanation the user must read to proceed. Pure extraneous load - if the label had been clear, this would be zero. Do not charge for text the user could skip and still succeed.

The Decision component is scored at 1.0 per bit, so each decision-* weight is just log2(n+1). Two options is log2(3) = 1.58. Charge it at every genuine fork, including the ones with no visible control.

Bucket default at n=5: log2(6) = 2.58. When you know the real option count, compute log2(n+1) and use that instead - the buckets exist for when the count is fuzzy, not to replace arithmetic you can do.

Bucket default at n=12: log2(13) = 3.70. DOUBLE it when the user must read and comprehend each option rather than recognise it at a glance - for unfamiliar terms the cost is closer to linear than logarithmic, and the log understates it badly.

These weights are tunable and carry no more precision than the word calibration admits. What matters is that the SAME weights are used on both sides of a before/after comparison - a 40-point drop is a real claim, a 40-point total on its own is not. Change a weight if your product's evidence says so, then re-score both sides.
